extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners interested in the theory and production of comedy/humour (literary critics, playwrights, comic artists)
extracted.subtask_description: A philosophical/literary analysis of what makes things laughable and which features of persons, gestures, forms and situations produce comic effects. Useful for scholars, writers, and performers seeking principled criteria for creating or evaluating humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic is strictly human
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic does not exist outside the pale of what is strictly HUMAN.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may laugh at an animal or an object only because you detect in it some human attitude or expression (e.g., a hat is laughable insofar as it embodies a human caprice). This criterion excludes landscapes and non-human phenomena unless they bear a human stamp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of feeling / disinterested spectator
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter usually accompanies an ABSENCE OF FEELING; the comic requires a momentary anesthesia of the heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The spectator must impose silence on pity/affection and appeal to intelligence alone. Highly emotional engagement with a scene tends to extinguish laughter; disinterested, calm observation allows the comic to appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social nature of laughter / need for an echo
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is always the laughter of a group and needs an echo; it presupposes complicity with other laughers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic effects often travel within a closed social circle; many jokes that make one group laugh fail to translate across cultures because they depend on shared customs and ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as social gesture / corrective function
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter serves a SOCIAL signification: a gesture by which society restrains eccentricity and inelasticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond aesthetic pleasure, laughter functions utilitarianly to 'soften down' mechanical inelasticity of character and to encourage sociability — it punishes or discourages eccentric rigidity by ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic rooted in mechanical inelasticity / automatism
rubrics_metrics.description: The laughable element often consists of a certain MECHANICAL INELASTICITY or automatism where living adaptability is expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a runner who falls because his muscles continue the same movement (momentum/rigidity); a victim of a practical joke who continues like a machine. The comic arises where habit or rigidity fails to adapt to changing circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidental versus inherent comic; internalisation of mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic is originally accidental (external circumstances reveal inelasticity) but becomes deeper when the mechanical quality is internal to the person (e.g., systematic absentmindedness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the cause of mechanical behaviour is part of the person's inner life, the comic is more sustained and richer (e.g., a habitual absent-minded person vs. a one-off stumble).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: the more natural/transparent the cause, the more comic the effect
rubrics_metrics.description: When a comic effect's origin is natural and intelligible, the effect is more laughable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If absentmindedness or a vice can be traced to a concrete, comprehensible cause (e.g., devotion to romance causing daydreaming), the accumulation and intelligibility of mishaps amplify the comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absentmindedness as a primary comic source
rubrics_metrics.description: Absentmindedness (thinking of the past or imaginary situations rather than present reality) is contiguous to the fountain-head of the comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absentminded characters are comic because they act according to a past or imagined situation; comic authors exploit this for repeated, coherent mishaps that grow cumulatively funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic vice vs tragic vice
rubrics_metrics.description: A vice is comic when it is an external rigidity imposed on character (a 'ready-made frame') rather than deeply assimilated passion; such vices remain recognisable as types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic vices simplify and dominate the person without fully incorporating into personality; they remain a common noun (e.g., 'the miser') and can be ridiculed, whereas tragic vices are fully integrated and elicit different responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconsciousness of the comic person
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic person is generally comic in proportion to his ignorance of himself; consciousness of ridicule undermines the comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once a person knows he is ridiculous he will try to modify or hide the defect; comic effect depends on the subject's unawareness, which allows automatisms to operate visibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic physiognomy: fixed grimace and rigidity
rubrics_metrics.description: A laughable expression is one that suggests rigidity or a permanent grimace — a face that promises nothing more than it shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic expressions imply a personality absorbed into a mechanical action (e.g., always appearing to be laughing, weeping). The more a face looks like it could be imitated by a 'normally built person', the more the deformity can become comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caricature as revealing embryonic distortions (exaggeration as means)
rubrics_metrics.description: Caricature detects and magnifies tendencies already present in nature; exaggeration must function as a means to make distortions visible, not as an end in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A caricature is comic when it amplifies an already latent inclination (e.g., lengthening a nose in the direction nature tended to lengthen it), thereby making the face 'grimace' more clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic contrasted with gracefulness (rigidness not ugliness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic is better contrasted with gracefulness than with ugliness; it belongs to rigidness or stereotypy rather than to mere unsightliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What makes us laugh is the petrification of movement/pose (loss of supple animation), not necessarily sheer ugliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gestures and movements laughable to the degree they suggest a machine
rubrics_metrics.description: ATTITUDES, GESTURES AND MOVEMENTS ARE LAUGHABLE IN EXACT PROPORTION AS THAT BODY REMINDS US OF A MERE MACHINE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A gesture that repeats, is uniform, or seems mechanically determined (e.g., a public speaker's recurring head movement) produces laughter because it betrays automatism within life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition / mechanical uniformity produces laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: A movement that returns at regular intervals and can be expected elicits laughter because it exposes a machine-like routine within a living being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic effect increases when spectators can wait for and predict the gesture; the expectation of a repeated mechanical action deflects life toward the mechanical in the spectator's mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation reveals automatism and becomes laughable
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation of gestures makes them laughable by bringing out their mechanical uniformity; to imitate is to expose what is alien to living personality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody that deflects gestures toward simple mechanical occupations (sawing, tugging a rope) heightens the sense of automatism and therefore the comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity / uniformity amplifies comic (marionette effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: When several persons act in the same mechanical way, we think of marionettes; absolute uniformity stiffens bodies into automata and heightens comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staging multiple identical gestures or synchronized actions makes the mechanical suggestion blatant and increases laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic/comedic devices derive from presenting human events as clockwork
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage devices (periodic repetition, systematic inversion, geometric development of farce) derive comic force from showing an obvious clockwork arrangement of human events while preserving outward probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights' art consists in making human actions appear as a calculated mechanism yet retaining enough plausibility to keep a semblance of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fashion and disguise: comic when continuity broken
rubrics_metrics.description: Garments and fashions become laughable when a dissolution of continuity separates them from the person (disguise); many fashions are latently comic but become visible when discontinuity occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sudden clash between covering and covered (anachronistic dress, incongruous costume) draws attention to mechanical incompatibility and yields comic effect. Habit and custom can deaden the comic; a break revives it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latent comic vs comic de facto — role of custom and surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Many things are comic de jure (in principle) without being comic de facto because habit and custom have deadened the comic quality; a sudden dissolution of continuity is needed to make the comic manifest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanations of laughter by surprise or contrast alone are insufficient; the comic may be present but unnoticed until custom is broken and we are forced to see the mechanical incongruity.
